title: JavaScript engines and how V8 compiles code
hook: You do not ship machine code when you deploy JavaScript — the engine compiles it inside the running process. V8's Just-In-Time (JIT) pipeline is the classic interview topic: parse, bytecode, optimize hot functions, deoptimize when assumptions break.

blocks.text: A JavaScript engine is the component that turns your source text into running behavior. V8 (used in Chrome and Node.js) parses JavaScript into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), generates bytecode with an interpreter (Ignition), and promotes frequently executed functions to optimized machine code via a JIT compiler (TurboFan). If runtime types diverge from what the optimizer assumed, V8 deoptimizes back to bytecode. Other engines — SpiderMonkey (Firefox), JavaScriptCore (Safari) — follow similar ideas with different names. This is unlike C#, where Roslyn emits IL at build time and the CLR's tiered JIT compiles methods before or during execution with metadata the engine always trusts.

entries.plainDefinition: Compiling code to machine instructions while the program is already running, usually after observing which paths are hot.
entries.example: A loop that runs ten thousand times triggers TurboFan optimization in V8.

entries.plainDefinition: A tree representation of source code structure after parsing. The engine walks the AST to generate bytecode or machine code.
entries.example: A function declaration becomes a node with parameters and a body subtree.

entries.plainDefinition: When optimized machine code assumed stable types or shapes that changed, V8 throws away the optimized code and falls back to slower bytecode.
entries.example: Passing a string into a function that was optimized for numbers triggers deopt.

blocks.text: Performance surprises in JavaScript often come from the engine, not from "interpreted vs compiled" slogans. Cold code runs slower in bytecode; hot loops become native code. Changing object shapes after optimization — adding properties in different orders, mixing types in the same variable — can cause repeated deopts and hurt throughput. In C#, tiered JIT also warms up, but CLR metadata gives the JIT stable type information JavaScript lacks. Benchmarking JavaScript without warm-up misleads you; benchmarking right after deploy measures interpreter speed, not peak JIT speed.

blocks.title: Interview one-liner
blocks.body: Modern JavaScript is JIT-compiled, not purely interpreted. V8: parse → Ignition bytecode → TurboFan for hot code → deopt on type/shape changes.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Parse source to AST
items.body: Lexer and parser build a syntax tree. Syntax errors fail here before any code runs.

items.title: Ignition generates bytecode
items.body: Bytecode executes immediately — fast startup, lower peak speed. Every function starts here.

items.title: Profiler marks hot functions
items.body: Counters track how often bytecode runs. Hot functions queue for TurboFan.

items.title: TurboFan emits optimized machine code
items.body: Assumes stable types and object shapes (hidden classes). Inlined property access becomes direct memory offsets.

items.title: Deoptimize on assumption break
items.body: Wrong type or mutated shape invalidates optimized code. Execution resumes in bytecode until maybe re-optimized.

diagram.title: V8 JIT pipeline vs CLR tiered JIT
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  JS[JavaScript source] --> Parse[Parser / AST]
  Parse --> Ignition[Ignition bytecode]
  Ignition --> Hot{Hot enough?}
  Hot -->|yes| TurboFan[TurboFan optimized code]
  Hot -->|no| Ignition
  TurboFan --> Deopt{Assumptions hold?}
  Deopt -->|no| Ignition
  Deopt -->|yes| TurboFan
  CS[C# IL] --> CLRJIT[CLR tiered JIT]
  CLRJIT --> Native[Native code with metadata]

snippet.label: Hot loop gets optimized
snippet.explanation: After enough calls with numeric arrays, V8 compiles `sumNumbers` to fast machine code. First calls run in Ignition bytecode — benchmark only the steady state after warm-up.

snippet.label: Deoptimization from type change
snippet.explanation: V8 may specialize `+` for numbers. Feeding strings later still produces correct `'12'`, but the optimizer may bail out to generic bytecode. Polymorphic call sites are slower than monomorphic ones.

snippet.label: Hidden classes and property order
snippet.explanation: V8 groups objects with the same property layout into hidden classes. Consistent construction order keeps shapes stable. C# structs and classes have fixed layout from compile-time metadata — no equivalent surprise at run time.

snippet.label: Measuring with warm-up
snippet.explanation: Production servers and long-lived tabs hit optimized code. Micro-benchmarks without warm-up measure Ignition, not TurboFan — similar to measuring CLR Tier-0 JIT and calling it final performance.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Calling JavaScript "interpreted only" — V8 JIT-compiles hot code. Assuming `node --version` tells you optimization behavior without warm-up benchmarks. Optimizing object shapes in one code path then breaking them in another (different property order). Comparing first-run Node latency to warmed-up .NET without acknowledging both use JIT.

interviewTakeaways: V8 pipeline: parse → AST → Ignition bytecode → TurboFan for hot functions → deoptimize when assumptions break.
Hidden classes reward consistent object layout; polymorphic types at the same call site hurt optimization.
Always warm up before benchmarking JavaScript — cold bytecode is not steady-state production performance.
60s: JS engines JIT at run time. V8 starts in bytecode, optimizes hot paths with TurboFan, deopts on type or shape changes. CLR JIT has IL metadata upfront. TS adds no run-time type help.
Follow-up: what is a hidden class and why does property order matter?
commonPitfalls: Saying JavaScript is never compiled — modern engines JIT-compile hot functions aggressively.
Benchmarking cold first invocation and claiming it represents production throughput.
Strong answer: 'Parse, bytecode, profile, TurboFan, deopt on shape/type change. Warm up benchmarks. CLR has metadata; V8 infers.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: C# comparison: Both V8 and the CLR use tiered compilation, but CLR trusts IL type metadata while V8 must speculate from observed values. Deoptimization is far more common in JavaScript.
TypeScript annotations do not reach V8. `const n: number = x` erases to `const n = x` — the JIT still discovers types dynamically.
